name: Friulian
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Miotti, Renzo. 2002. Friulian (Illustrations of the IPA). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 32(2): 237-247. doi:10.1017/S0025100302001056
catalog_locator: Section 'Stress and rhythm', pp. 244-245 (pp. 8-9); clitic statement in 'Intonation', p. 245; speaker/variety statement p. 237; length-mark paradigm ('/Vː/ is [VV] or [VˑV].. /V/ is realized as [Vˑ] or [Vː]') p. 244
catalog_quote: Stress in central Friulian may fall on any of the word's last four syllables, as in cjacarâ /cakaˈraː/ 'to chat', tu cjacaris /tucaˈkaris/ 'you chat', lis cjacaris /lisˈcakaris/ 'the chats', dânusindi /ˈdaːnusindi/ 'to give us some'. Accents on the fourth last syllable are, however, rather rare and normally limited to certain verb + clitic combinations. The position of the stress is phonemically relevant in Friulian, its location being unpredictable. This is illustrated in the transcriptions above as well as minimal pairs like the following: (a) cjantin /ˈcantin/ 'they sing' vs. (o) cjantìn /canˈtin/ 'we sing'. Friulian words carry only one primary stress but, in polysyllables, a secondary stress may appear on the most peripheral unstressed syllable, usually when preceding the stressed one: cjacarâ [ˌcakaˈɾaˑ]. The occurrence of such a secondary stress normally depends on the rhythmic context in which the words are found. Stressed syllables are longer than unstressed ones, but the length of the stressed vowel is determined by two main factors – the structure of the syllable and the characteristics of the following segment (see the section on vowels above).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is lexically fixed and contrastive; it can fall on the final, penultimate, antepenultimate or (rarely, only with enclitics) pre-antepenultimate syllable, and its position cannot be predicted from the phonological shape of the word. Final (oxytone) stress is the most frequent pattern and antepenultimate is rare (Carrozzo 2008: 22); disyllables default to penultimate stress in the orthographic conventions (Pirona 1871: XXIX). Written grave/circumflex accents mark the stressed vowel where needed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: A rhythmic secondary stress may appear on the most peripheral unstressed syllable, usually the initial pretonic one (cjacarâ [ˌcakaˈɾaː]); its occurrence depends on the rhythmic context (Miotti 2002: 245).
new_statements.exceptions: Fourth-last-syllable stress is rare and normally limited to verb + clitic combinations (dânusindi). Carrozzo 2008 p. 22 adds that reference-Friulian verb forms (except with enclitic pronouns) cannot be proparoxytone, and that oxytones are very frequent while proparoxytones are fairly rare; Marchetti 1952 p. 26 says general rules for Friulian accentuation are practically impossible to state.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word including clitics: 'clitics.. are grouped under the stress of the word to which they are attached', p. 246); citation forms and connected speech both illustrated. Describes central Friulian (basis of the koine), explicitly excluding the Udine city variety.
new_statements.identity_note: Miotti 2002 describes central Friulian (the basis of the koine and official standard), explicitly excluding the Udine city variety; Carrozzo 2000/2008 and Marchetti 1952 describe the reference/koine variety ('furlan di riferiment'). All map to the language-level glottocode friu1240; Carrozzo notes that some northern (Carnic) varieties allow proparoxytone verb forms that the reference variety does not.

sources.citation: Carrozzo, Sandri (Alessandro). 2008. Gramatiche fonetiche furlane. [2nd ed., in Friulian]. Section 3.2 'Vocâls tonichis e vocâls atonis', pp. 21-22
sources.note: Every word normally has one tonic vowel; words with final stress are called 'concjadis', penultimate 'planis', antepenultimate 'sbrissulis'; if a word is unknown and has no written accent, the stress must be looked up in a pronouncing dictionary, but oxytones are very frequent and proparoxytones fairly rare; reference-Friulian verb forms (except with enclitic pronouns) cannot be proparoxytone. Only tonic vowels take grave/circumflex marks.

sources.citation: Marchetti, Giuseppe. 1952. Lineamenti di grammatica friulana. Udine: Società Filologica Friulana. Section 'La grafia', §4 'Gli accenti', p. 26
sources.note: 'riuscirebbe pressoché impossibile dettare delle norme generali sull'accentazione friulana' (it would be almost impossible to state general rules for Friulian stress placement); stress is distinctive (massàrie/massarie, pòdin/podìn, fàsin/fasìn); rest is orthographic accent-marking policy.

sources.citation: Pirona, Jacopo. 1871. Vocabolario friulano. Venezia: Antonelli. Introduction, 'Accentuazione', pp. XXIX-XXX
sources.note: Orthographic accent rules: accent may be omitted on the penult of most disyllables (i.e., penultimate is the default reading), and on the final syllable of polysyllables ending in a double consonant or two different consonants, 'since the force of those two consonants carries the emphasis of pronunciation onto that syllable'; otherwise every word should be accented.

sources.citation: della Porta, G. B. 1922. Grammatica friulana pratica. Udine: Del Bianco. §§2-4, pp. 1-2
sources.note: Orthographic rules only: a long final vowel always carries the stress and is written with circumflex; a written accent is required when a polysyllable ends in a stressed vowel. No general placement rule.
